title: Unconventional and Fragile Magnetic Exciton in a van der Waals Quantum Magnet
authors: Kai-Xuan Zhang, Min Zhang, Minjae Kim, Yong-Hyun Kim, Junghyun Kim, Heejun Yang, Pyeongjae Park, Chaebin Kim, Mangesh Diware, Junik Hwang, Youjin Lee, Byeong-Gwan Cho, Hyeong-Do Kim, Tae-Yeong Koo, Chunhua Chen, Mingtao Li, Xujie Lü, Wenge Yang, Kee-Hoon Kim, Seung-Ho Baek, Hyeonsik Cheong, Sung-Keun Lee, Beom Hyun Kim, Christopher Lane, Jian-Xin Zhu, Zhaorong Yang, Young-Woo Son, Je-Geun Park
abstract: The recently discovered magnetic exciton in the van der Waals (vdW) antiferromagnet NiPS3 exemplifies these phenomena, exhibiting several distinctive characteristics. Despite extensive investigation, much of its physics remains unresolved, with key questions about why the NiPS3 magnetic exciton is so sharp and optically bright despite the nominally spin-forbidden transition, posing significant challenges to a proper understanding and practical manipulation of the exciton. An urgent question is to what extent it is due to chemical disorder, magnetic weakening, lattice modification, or intrinsic instability of the bright exciton itself: answers to which will put stringent constraints on possible theoretical models. Here we address these questions using hydrostatic pressure as a clean, continuous, reversible, and in-situ tuning parameter. We find that the sharp photoluminescence peak is drastically suppressed by as little as 0.4 GPa and completely quenched by 1.5 GPa, with demonstrating its reversibility. Crucially, this bright-to-dark conversion occurs without magnetic, crystallographic, or electronic reconstruction despite an increase in the Neel temperature, as established by Raman, X-ray absorption, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and first-principles many-body calculations. Our results demonstrate that the optical brightness of the magnetic exciton is independent of chemical disorder, lattice expansion, and weakening of magnetic order, indicating that a higher-order correlated mechanism governs the bright exciton. We further propose experimentally constrained microscopic scenarios involving exciton pairing, crystal-field-controlled spin-orbit mixing, and symmetry breaking, providing a framework for future tests of entangled magnetic exciton in correlated quantum magnets.
summary: This paper investigates the fragile nature of a magnetic exciton in NiPS3 using hydrostatic pressure as a tuning tool. By showing that the exciton's sharp photoluminescence is quenched at low pressures without structural changes, the authors argue against simple disorder or lattice effects. They propose that a higher-order correlated mechanism, involving crystal field splitting and symmetry breaking, governs this fascinating quantum optical phenomenon.
main_problem: The study aims to resolve the origin of the sharp, optically bright magnetic exciton in NiPS3, particularly understanding why this transition remains bright despite being nominally spin-forbidden.
main_result: The optical brightness is shown to be independent of chemical disorder or lattice expansion, suggesting a higher-order correlated mechanism governs the exciton's stability. The exciton undergoes complete quenching at low pressures (1.5 GPa) without structural reconstruction.
method: The research combines high-pressure experimental measurements (PL, Raman, XAS, NMR) with first-principles many-body calculations to probe the system's response to external tuning parameters.
model_or_system: The physical system is the van der Waals antiferromagnet NiPS3. The model involves excitons arising from transitions between Zhang-Rice triplet (ZRT) and singlet (ZRS) states, analyzed using concepts like paired ZRS (PZRS) states.
key_observables: Photoluminescence peak intensity/energy, Neel temperature ($T_N$), Raman phonon modes, XAS pre-edge features, and the pressure dependence of these quantities.
important_parameters: Hydrostatic pressure (up to 1.5 GPa), Temperature, Exciton energy ($\sim 1.47 	ext{ eV}$), Crystal field splitting ($\Delta_{10Dq}$).
main_assumptions: The initial assumption is that the exciton's behavior can be mapped onto structural or magnetic changes; this is challenged by showing PL suppression occurs without such reconstruction.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate PL peak suppression and redshift under pressure, comparison of Raman/XAS spectra across pressures, and conceptual diagrams detailing mechanisms like PZRS states, crystal field splitting enhancement, and symmetry breaking via $A_{1g}^{(1)}$ phonons.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the mystery (bright exciton in NiPS3), uses hydrostatic pressure as a clean tuning parameter to test hypotheses (disorder vs. intrinsic instability), presents evidence ruling out structural/electronic changes (Raman, XAS, NMR), and concludes by proposing higher-order correlated mechanisms involving symmetry breaking.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed case study of how external pressure can tune the coherence and visibility of an excitonic state in a strongly correlated magnetic material, linking optical properties to underlying quantum mechanical symmetries and correlations.
